summary:
Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France.

Same-sex marriage reached Réunion with the statute adopted in France in 2013, following the bill announced by Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault in October 2012 for passage through the National Assembly and the Senate, which delivered President François Hollande's campaign pledge. Both houses had to approve the text.

Discrimination on the ground of 'identité sexuelle' has been prosecutable in France since the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 in July 2012, making transphobic harassment a criminal matter; deputies Sergio Coronado and Elisabeth Pochon intervened in that debate. The term was replaced by 'gender identity' through amendment of article 225-1 on 18 November 2016, with parallel protection added in the Labour Code.

Legal gender change rests on the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282, adopted by the National Assembly on 19 May 2016 after being tabled by roughly forty Socialist deputies, though the government's three sub-amendments could limit its scope. The regime took effect on 1 January 2017 after Senate approval on 6 November 2015, Assembly approvals on 24 May 2016, 12 July 2016 and 12 October 2016, a Constitutional Council ruling of constitutionality on 17 November 2016 and signature on 18 November 2016 with publication the following day. It requires an application before a court without psychiatrist certificates or proof of reassignment surgery; a first-name change can be handled at the registry office.

In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness by decree, though transgender rights organisations stated that nothing changed beyond the announcement, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 and treatment funded by the Sécurité Sociale. Gender-affirming surgery within France was legalised in 1979.

In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by imprisonment. A report of 16 May 2020 recorded police identification of around 1,870 victims of transphobic and homophobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018; these are raw national counts without a per-capita denominator.

Prison placement in France follows the sex recorded on the identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code. Transgender women held in male prisons therefore fall into a legal grey area and are, in the account of a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018, 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes'; the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. The placement rule is the framework that governs detainees in Réunion.

The French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL) found 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities in its opinion of 25 May 2021. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site and documentary inspections, and it carries recommendations addressed to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. The opinion applies to the national framework covering Réunion.

Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces. Conversion therapy was banned by a bill passed by the Senate on 7 December 2020, concurred by the Assembly on 25 January 2022 and published on 1 February 2022, with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or a 30,000 euro fine.

In March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education announced that institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms.

A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access to care by location, and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The National Academy of Medicine has characterised increased treatment-seeking as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution without changing actual practice. A March 2024 Senate-commissioned report led to a Senate-passed May 2024 bill to ban medical transition under 18, opposed by the Macron government and unlikely to pass the Assembly, with no update since 23 July 2024. In late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D supplements.
tangentialFactors:
France's anti-discrimination machinery includes the High Authority against Discrimination and for Equality, created by the December 2004 law, and the Ministry of Education's January 2019 Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign with reporting services, a helpline and LGBTQ guidance, alongside observance of 17 May.

The law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic comments illegal, punishable by up to a 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred, violence or discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation or disability; physical assault or murder motivated by sexual orientation carries increased penalties.

National legislation prohibiting sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and goods and services was enacted in 1985 and incorporated in the Labour Code. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) were enacted in 1999 for same-sex and unmarried opposite-sex couples, affording most marriage protections.

A ban on men who have sex with men donating blood dating to 20 June 1983 was recalled on 12 January 2009, replaced by a one-year abstinence rule effective 10 July 2016, reduced to four months from 2 April 2020, then removed on 16 March 2022, applying the same policy regardless of sexual orientation. In March 2024 the Assembly unanimously passed a bill for compensation to gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980, pending Senate vote.

Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 with no mention of same-sex relations in private, retained in the Penal Code of 1810 and followed in French colonies adopting the Code. A discriminatory age of consent of 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual, introduced 6 August 1942 and lowered to 18 in 1974, was repealed 4 August 1982 to equalise at 15; a 1960 provision doubling the penalty for homosexual indecent exposure under article 330 alinea 2 was repealed in 1980.

France became the thirteenth country to legalise same-sex marriage through a bill approved by the Assembly on 12 February 2013 by 329-229 and the Senate on 12 April 2013, ruled constitutional 17 May 2013, signed 18 May 2013 with the first ceremony on 29 May in Montpellier, with joint adoption legal since May 2013. The Catholic Bishops Conference came out against adoption when the bill was announced in 2012.
